Briefly put, the case of the prosecution is that on 20.01.2016, at about 10:15 PM, at Maharishi Raman Marg crossing Lodhi Road, New Delhi within the jurisdiction of PS Tughlak Road, accused Ashish Jaiswal FIR No.10/2016 (State vs. Ashish Jaiswal) PS Sagarpur was found driving the offending vehicle (Eco Sports car) bearing no. Additionally, a challan under Sec. 146/196 MV Act was filed against the owner of the offending vehicle, Dr. Yashwardhan Jaiswal for failure to produce valid insurance policy qua the offending vehicle.

INGREDIENTS OF THE OFFENCE- 10.
Before dwelling into the facts of the present case, it would be apposite to discuss the legal standards required to be met.
The gravamen of the offence under Section 279 IPC is the act of the accused, done with "rashness" or "negligence".
The IPC does not define either of these terms.
However, the ambit of these terms has now been settled by judicial pronouncements of superior Courts.
In Empress of India vs. Idu Beg ILR (1881) 3 All 776 the term "rashness" was interpreted to mean commission of an act with indifference or recklessness towards the consequences of such act.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Rathnashalvan vs. State of Karnataka (2007) 3 SCC 474 has observed, inter alia, as under-:
"7. ....

sentences.text: Culpable negligence lies in the failure to exercise reasonable and proper care and the extent of its reasonableness will always depend upon the circumstances of each case.
Rashness means doing an act with the consciousness of a risk that evil consequences will follow but with the hope that it will not.
Negligence is a breach of duty imposed by law.
In criminal cases, the amount and degree of negligence are determining factors.

A question whether the accused's conduct amounted to culpable rashness or negligence depends directly on the question as to what is the amount of care and circumspection which a prudent and reasonable man would consider it to be sufficient considering all the circumstances of the case.

Criminal rashness means hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is dangerous or Fir No.10/2016 (State vs . Ashish Jaiswal) Ps Sagarpur on 19 August, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109115974/
9 wanton and the further knowledge that it may cause injury but done without any intention to cause injury or knowledge that it would probably be caused.

sentences.text: . As noted above, "rashness" consists in hazarding a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is so, and that it may cause injury.
The criminality lies in such a case in running the risk of doing such an act with recklessness or indifference as to the consequences.

Criminal negligence on the other hand, is the gross and culpable neglect or failure to exercise that reasonable and proper care and precaution to guard against injury either to the public generally or to an individual in particular, which,
having regard to all the circumstances out of which the charge has arisen it was the imperative duty of the accused person to have adopted."
Similar observations were made by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Sushil Ansal vs. CBI (2014) 6 SCC 173.

The standard of negligence was discussed in the said case, by observing, inter alia,
as under-:
"58.

In the case of "negligence" the courts have favoured a meaning which implies a gross and culpable neglect or failure to exercise that reasonable and proper care and precaution to guard against injury either to the public generally or to an individual which having regard to all the circumstances out of which the charge arises, it may be the imperative duty of the accused to have adopted.

Negligence has been understood to be an omission to do something which a reasonable man guided upon those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person would not do.

Unlike rashness, where the imputability arises from acting despite the consciousness,
negligence implies acting without such consciousness, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon him.
The imputability in the case of negligence arises from the neglect of the civil duty of circumspection."
Thus, rashness implies doing an act despite the consciousness that it might result in injuries.
Negligence, on the other hand, means lack of reasonable care that a person placed in the fact situation ought to take, in order to avoid injuries.

11. Thus, in order to establish the offence under Section 279 of the IPC, the prosecution has to prove that the accused was driving the offending vehicle on a public way in a "rash" or "negligent" manner,
so as to endanger human life or cause hurt/injury to any person.

However, even FIR No.10/2016 (State vs. Ashish Jaiswal) PS Sagarpur before 'rashness' and 'negligence' can be imputed upon the accused, it is essential for the prosecution to prove that the accused was in fact driving the offending vehicle at the time of the accident.

However, this Court is not in agreement with this argument of the Ld. APP as the law is trite that confession made to a police officer is inadmissible in law (Section 25, Indian Evidence Act).

Further,
in criminal law, the burden of proof on the prosecution is that of beyond reasonable doubt.
The presumption of innocence of the accused has to be rebutted by the prosecution by adducing cogent evidence that points towards the guilt of the accused.
In other words, the onus of proving all the essential ingredients of an offence is always upon the prosecution and at no stage does it shift to the accused.

13. Thus, in order to prove, the accused as driver of the offending vehicle, the prosecution has examined two witnesses- PW1/injured Ram Kishore; and PW6/Shantanu Bhadoo, who is stated to be an eye witness to the incident.

14. Perusal of the testimonies on record reveals that the accused was not identified as driver of the offending vehicle, during trial either by PW1/injured Ram Kishore or PW6/Eye-witness Shantanu Bhadoo.

PW1/ injured Ram Kishore categorically deposed before the Court that on ac- count of having sustained injuries due to the accident, he lost consciousness FIR No.10/2016 (State vs.
Ashish Jaiswal) PS Sagarpur soon after the accident and failed to see the driver of the offending vehicle.
Further, PW6/Eye-witness Shantanu Bhadoo didn't support the case of the prosecution, as he denied being an eyewitness to the accident and was hence, declared hostile.
PW6/Shantanu Bhadoo has deposed before the court that he correctly identify the accused only because he saw him during trial, previously appearing on court dates.
15. It is pertinent to note that under Indian law, the evidence of hostile witnesses is not discarded completely.
The legal maxim, "false in uno false in omnibus" is not applicable in India.
With respect to the evidentiary value of hostile witnesses, it was observed by the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Rohtash Kumar v. State of Haryana, (2013) 14 SCC 434, as under - "25.

16. Therefore, it has to be seen if the evidence of such hostile witnesses can be relied in part.
However, PW-6 failed to depose anything at all in favour of the prosecution.
He denied being an eye-witness to the accident.
He stated that the accident had already taken place before he reached the spot.
He denied that he identified the accused as driver of the offending vehicle, before the police.
He denied that the accused was arrested by the IO in his presence.
He denied that the arrest memo of the accused was prepared in his presence.
He failed to identify both, the offending as well as the offended vehicle.

sentences.text: No other independent eyewitness of the incident has been cited by the prosecution.
There is no other circumstance or clinching piece of evidence such as CCTV footage, mentioned in the chargesheet, that points towards the guilt of the accused.

17. Thus, even if the evidence of the hostile witness/PW6 Shantanu Bhadoo is considered partly,
there is nothing to implicate the accused Ashish Jaiswal.

All the other remaining witnesses are either formal witnesses or police witnesses and none of them is a witness to the accident, sufficient only to prove that PW1/Ram Kishore had received injuries, pursuant to which an FIR with respect to the said incident was lodged at PS Tughlaq Road vide FIR bearing No. 10/2016 and investigation was conducted thereupon.
The prosecution has NOT successfully proved that the accident was caused by the accused Ashish Jaiswal by driving vehicle bearing number UP53BK6996, in a rash and negligent manner.
The testimony of all the remaining witnesses together, is insufficient to prove the allegations against the accused qua offence u/s. 279 IPC.

Thus, there is nothing on record to connect the accused with the commission of the offence u/s. 279 IPC.
18.

In the event of the failure of the prosecution to prove the identity of the accused as driver of the offending vehicle on the date of the incident, the offence of traffic violation (red-light jumping) u/s.
119/177 M.V. Act also cannot be proved against the accused.

This is because the main eye-witness of the prosecution i.e. PW6/Shantanu Bhadoo has turned hostile during his examination at trial and no independent evidence FIR No.10/2016 (State vs. Ashish Jaiswal) PS Sagarpur including CCTV footage has been produced by the prosecution to prove that the accused being driver of the offending vehicle, violated traffic signal on the date of the incident.
The deficiencies in the case of the prosecution have dragged the case of the prosecution significantly within the ambit of reasonable doubts, the benefit of which has to be extended to the accused.

19. To recapitulate the above discussion, to bring home the guilt of the accused for the offence u/s.
279 IPC and offence u/s. 119/177 M.V. Act, the prosecution was required to prove the offences beyond reasonable doubt, which essentially includes proving the identity of accused as driver of the offending vehicle.

Therefore, there is no evidence to link the accused with the crime charged against him.
The ingredients of the offence u/s. 279 IPC and offence u/s. 119/177 M.V. Act, are not fulfilled from the material on record.

20. Further, as already stated above, statement of compounding was preferred by the complainant for the offence u/s. 338 IPC.
